The last amber sliver of sun grazes the ridgeline, throwing violet shadow-rivers down through the standing timber.

A pale lemon dawn seeps between trunks, the light almost liquid, falling in slow tilted panels across the forest floor.
Blood-orange dusk fires the underside of the cloud shelf, the path below it washed in deep persimmon and umber.
Silver pre-dawn, the sky barely lighter than the trees, everything holding its breath in a soft pewter suspension.
God-rays push through the morning mist in thick warm shafts, each beam made visible by hanging moisture and drifting pollen.
The green world goes amber for twenty minutes at day's end, shadows stretching longer than the trees that cast them.

First light catches the top third of the oaks gold while the path beneath them remains in blue pre-morning shadow.

Crepuscular rays fan down through a break in the ridge-cloud, spotlighting patches of the wet track in pale gold columns.

The fog-diffused morning sun has no single source, the light arriving from everywhere at once in an even warm-white glow.
Dusk drops the temperature of the light ten degrees in ten minutes, warm gold curdling quickly into cool blue-violet.
A low autumn sun burns orange at the path's end, reduced by haze to a visible disc, tolerable to look at.
The hour after sunrise, hard shadows still short, the light still carrying the thin cool sweetness of the night just gone.

Rose-gold dawn bleeding through river mist, painting the path amber while blue shadow still holds the hollows.
Blood-orange dusk casting long warm streaks across the stones, cool violet pooling beneath the ancient oaks.
Pale silver pre-dawn light, the sky neither night nor morning, every surface holding a cold luminous grey.
Amber gloaming settling into the valley, the last warmth of sun caught in the treetops while the ground goes blue.
God-rays driving through fog at first light, columns of rose-gold fire cutting the grey like slow-moving breath.
Lavender blue-hour draping the hillside, the horizon still faintly orange while overhead the sky deepens to cool indigo.
Thin golden last-light grazing the path sideways, every pebble casting a shadow ten times its own length.
Foggy pale morning where the sun is only a rumor, diffused through white air into soft directionless warmth.

Blue-hour stillness, the sky a sheet of cold pewter-blue, the distant treeline lit faintly orange along its crown.
A low autumn sun pressing through river mist, the whole world amber and diffuse, shadows long and soft-edged.
Dusk turning the path to hammered copper, long blue shadows reaching east while the western sky bleeds red.
First dawn light catching the fog in layers, each tree emerging amber then gold then finally clear and warm.
The green flash dying on the horizon, leaving the path bathed in one final second of pure golden warmth.
Soft rose morning, cloud-filtered and gentle, the light arriving sideways through the pines in pale warm ribbons.
Amber late-afternoon slant, the sun an hour from setting, every surface gilded and every shadow stretched into blue.
Cold silver transitional light, the precise moment between dusk and true dark, the sky holding faint peach at its edge.
Dawn mist glowing from within, the unseen sun backlighting fog into walls of warm translucent gold.
The last true light before blue-hour, golden and raking, turning ordinary gravel into a road of hammered fire.
Deep-amber gloaming on the marshpath, warm light dying in the reeds while cool blue climbs up from the water.
A blood-red sun resting on the treeline, too low to illuminate, only to silhouette and rim everything in fire.
Pre-dawn blue, not dark but not light, the path visible in cold pewter tones before any warmth arrives.
Long golden shadows of late afternoon, parallel bars of warm and cool alternating across the earth like slow music.
Thin winter dawn, pale amber barely cresting the ridge, every frosted surface catching the light in cold rose fire.
The amber last-light moment when the sun clears the clouds before setting, flooding everything horizontal in pure molten gold.
